item.title: Family breakdown among key factors behind street-connected children-Kiran
item.description: Family breakdown and emotional disconnection remain among the primary drivers of displacement among street-connected children. This was highlighted by Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran while speaking in Parliament, stressing people often ask what is being done to remove children from the streets, but the real question is why they are on the streets in the first place.
item.content:encoded:
Family breakdown and emotional disconnection remain among the primary drivers of displacement among street-connected children.

This was highlighted by Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran while speaking in Parliament, stressing people often ask what is being done to remove children from the streets, but the real question is why they are on the streets in the first place.

She says when children do not feel safe, valued or loved at home, they become increasingly vulnerable to exploitation by criminal and drug networks.

Drawing on her personal interactions with these children, she says many speak of family breakdown, parental abandonment, violence, neglect and profound emotional disconnection.

She says the Government is also establishing a specialised rehabilitation facility for street-connected children in Suva.

She says Fiji must reverse this reality and strengthen the traditional protective pillars of Fijian society.

She says active, emotionally present and nurturing parenting is essential in building the resilience and strength of character that children need to resist substance abuse and exploitation.

Kiran says Fiji must revive its traditional support systems.

Through a whole-of-government approach and in partnership with UNICEF Pacific, she says Bebbo Pacific, Fiji's first free digital parenting application, has been launched.

She says the application supports Fiji's national early childhood development policy and provides practical guidance from pregnancy through to a child's sixth birthday.

Kiran shares more than 1,300 downloads were recorded within its first six weeks and described the initial response as highly encouraging.

She adds when strong foundations of love, values and open communication are built at home, children will have the confidence and resilience to resist harmful influences, adding that children should not need drug dealers or criminal networks to tell them that they matter and belong.

She says help is available and families can call the 24-hour toll-free helpline 5626 to seek support and assistance.

During the Bebbo Pacific awareness programme, she says grandparents showed officials games their grandchildren had downloaded on their phones saying they did not realise that some of these applications depict violence that is not age-appropriate and could influence behaviour from an early age.

Kiran also highlights the surge in alcohol and substance abuse among children is driving an alarming rise in mental health challenges, domestic violence, self-harm and violent crime.

Kiran says Fiji's geographic position as a transit point for international trafficking networks has meant highly addictive substances, particularly methamphetamine, have become alarmingly accessible to children.

Kiran says Fiji recorded 1,501 illicit substance cases in 2020, including 100 cases involving methamphetamine and four involving cocaine.

She says most concerning of all is that children as young as 10 to 14 years old are now becoming trapped in the cycle of addiction.

Kiran says Fiji has witnessed rising youth mortality, an increase in crime and growing public health risks, including HIV transmission through shared needles.

She says there have also been ineffective treatment outcomes due to a shortage of specialist child psychologists and psychiatrists.

She says in partnership with Empower Pacific, Fiji's first dedicated residential recovery facility for adolescent boys aged 14 to 17 has been established.

She adds the facility, named Na Sala Vou Recovery Centre, provides a safe and structured environment where young men can heal, learn and rebuild their lives.

Kiran says the Government currently supports a transitional facility through the Kauwai Youth Restoration Centre, operated by the Salvation Army, which provides temporary care and support for vulnerable children identified as living on the streets.

Meanwhile, responding to the Minister’s statement, Opposition MP Virendra Lal questioned why so many young people are reaching the point where rehabilitation is required in the first place.

He says if resources are concentrated on treating young people after they become addicted, while the circumstances exposing them to drugs and alcohol are not addressed, Fiji will continue dealing with the consequences rather than the causes.

Lal also questioned the reach of Bebbo Pacific, saying technology can provide useful information and guidance, but an application on a mobile phone cannot replace an involved parent, counsellor, social worker or a functioning family support system.

He says the Government needs to ensure the initiative reaches the families who need assistance the most, noting that some vulnerable families may not know about the application, may have limited access to reliable internet services, or may require direct human assistance rather than information delivered through a screen.

Lal says young people facing substance abuse problems live throughout Fiji, including in rural and maritime communities, and the Government must explain how families in the Western Division, Northern Division and Maritime Islands will access appropriate rehabilitation and counselling services when their children need help.

item.title: Turaga outlines law reforms, Koya questions consultation process
item.description: A heated discussion erupted in Parliament this morning over Fiji’s law reform process, with the Opposition questioning the Government’s consultation process, planning and capacity to properly review the country’s laws. While delivering his statement, Acting Attorney General Siromi Turaga says the Fiji Law Reform Commission, re-established in 2023, is currently reviewing several laws, including the
item.content:encoded:
A heated discussion erupted in Parliament this morning over Fiji’s law reform process, with the Opposition questioning the Government’s consultation process, planning and capacity to properly review the country’s laws.

While delivering his statement, Acting Attorney General Siromi Turaga says the Fiji Law Reform Commission, re-established in 2023, is currently reviewing several laws, including the Civil Court Rules, High Court Rules, Magistrates’ Court Rules, Mining Act, Quarries Act, Online Safety Act, Security Industry Act and Human Trafficking Laws.

He says the Commission is also reviewing agriculture-related legislation dating as far back as 1877, as well as the Liquor Act 2006 and Liquor Regulations 2008.

Siromi - We are changing the laws Aug 19

Turaga says consultation is a fundamental part of responsible lawmaking and that several reviews were now moving through public consultation.

Opposition MP Faiyaz Koya says the Opposition supported the need for laws to be reviewed but challenged the Acting Attorney-General whether proper gap analysis, audits and consultation had been carried out before reforms were undertaken.

He questioned the Government’s approach to consultation, pointing to several bills which he claimed had not been thoroughly discussed with the public.

Koya - They don't consult people thorougly Aug 19

Koya specifically criticised changes to liquor licensing hours, saying the reduction in operating hours had raised concerns among small businesses that were still recovering from the COVID-19 pandemic.

He says the Government eventually reversed the decision, arguing the experience showed why the consequences of legislative changes needed to be properly identified through consultation before laws were amended.

Turaga also highlighted the review of Fiji’s electoral laws, saying the Commission had completed an electoral law reform package in 2025, including draft legislation and proposed changes to the country’s electoral framework.

item.title: Fiji strengthens humanitarian partnerships as disaster risks grow
item.description: Speaking during the commemoration of World Humanitarian Day , NDRMO Director Napolioni Boseiwaqa says Fiji’s humanitarian system depends on a whole-of-society approach, with Government working alongside civil society, volunteers, communities, development partners, the private sector and international organisations. He says Fiji continues to experience the impacts of cyclones, floods, droughts, cli
item.content:encoded:
Speaking during the commemoration of World Humanitarian Day , NDRMO Director Napolioni Boseiwaqa says Fiji’s humanitarian system depends on a whole-of-society approach, with Government working alongside civil society, volunteers, communities, development partners, the private sector and international organisations.

He says Fiji continues to experience the impacts of cyclones, floods, droughts, climate change, health emergencies and other crises , making strong coordination and preparedness essential.

Boseiwaqa acknowledges the contribution of humanitarian workers, volunteers and organisations who work to save lives, reduce suffering and protect the dignity of people affected by emergencies.

He also called for a moment of silence to remember humanitarian workers around the world who have lost their lives while serving communities in need .

The World Humanitarian Day event highlighted the growing risks faced by humanitarian workers globally, with more than a thousand humanitarian workers killed in the last three years, while many others have faced attacks, threats and violence.

Boseiwaqa says NDRMO is continuing work to strengthen Fiji’s humanitarian system through improved policies, better coordination mechanisms and stronger preparedness at national and community levels.

He says this includes the development of a Humanitarian Action Strategy and Volunteer Strategy to better recognise and support the contribution of volunteers.

Boseiwaqa also highlights the important role of organisations such as the Fiji Council of Social Services and the Fiji Red Cross Society in supporting vulnerable communities and strengthening locally-led humanitarian action.

He stresses that affected communities must remain at the centre of humanitarian response and thanked humanitarian partners, volunteers and organisations for their continued commitment to Fiji.

Meanwhile, Australian Diplomat Elizabeth Beard says protecting humanitarian workers and strengthening disaster preparedness remain critical as Fiji and the Pacific face growing risks from climate change and natural disasters.

Beard says this year’s World Humanitarian Day theme, “Act for Humanity,” highlights the increasing risks faced by humanitarian workers around the world and the need to protect humanitarian spaces.

She says humanitarian workers continue to provide vital assistance to communities affected by conflict, disasters and crises, often working in challenging and dangerous environments.

Beard says Australia, together with eight other countries, launched the Declaration for the Protection of Humanitarian Personnel in 2025 , which aims to strengthen protections for humanitarian workers and promote adherence to international legal frameworks.

She says Fiji’s endorsement of the declaration demonstrates a shared commitment between both countries to safeguard humanitarian personnel.

Beard also acknowledges the contribution of volunteers, first responders, community leaders, government officials and civil society organisations who play an important role in humanitarian action.

She says the Pacific is facing an increasingly complex risk environment, with El Niño-driven droughts, seasonal cyclones and the impacts of climate change placing greater pressure on communities, livelihoods and essential services.

Beard says humanitarian action is not only about responding after disasters occur, but also about strengthening resilience, improving preparedness and ensuring communities are ready before emergencies happen.

She highlights Australia’s ongoing support through the Vuvale Partnership with the Fiji Government and NDRMO to strengthen disaster preparedness and response systems.

Beard says Australia supports NDRMO’s training programmes, which build the skills and capabilities of humanitarian responders while improving the safety and protection of those involved in emergency response.

She adds that Australia values its partnerships with civil society organisations, faith-based groups, disability organisations and women’s organisations across Fiji.

Beard says effective humanitarian action must be locally-led, inclusive and built on the knowledge and strengths of communities themselves.

Also speaking at the event, Fiji Council of Social Services Executive Director Vani Catanasiga says communities, volunteers and civil society organisations have played a critical role in supporting Fiji during times of crisis and their contribution must continue to be recognised.

Catanasiga says Fiji’s experience during the challenging period between 2020 and 2022 showed that no single agency, ministry or sector could manage crises alone.

She says Fiji navigated those difficult times through strong collaboration between Government agencies, civil society organisations, academia, frontline volunteers and communities.

Catanasiga acknowledged NDRMO’s efforts in building relationships with community networks and volunteers, saying communities have recognised improvements in the agency’s engagement.

She referred to the FCOSS Kacivaka Scorecard , which assesses government agencies’ openness, and says NDRMO recorded improvements based on community feedback in 2021 and 2022.

However, Catanasiga raised concerns about some proposed disaster management regulations, saying they could create challenges for smaller community-based organisations, faith groups, youth groups and women’s networks.

She says requirements such as three years of independent audits and formal registration before operating could create barriers for local responders who are often the first to assist communities during disasters.

Catanasiga says some proposed suspension powers could also affect the independence of civil society organisations that provide important support to vulnerable communities.

She welcomed the formalisation of the humanitarian cluster system but said civil society organisations should be included in leadership roles to bring their experience and community knowledge into decision-making.
